data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is primarily caused by reduced radiative cooling due to the urban greenhouse effect: urban surfaces and pollutants re-absorb outgoing longwave radiation, and the single best cross-city modulator is the sky view factor determined by building height and street canyon geometry. Cities with deeper canyons trap more longwave radiation, producing a larger nocturnal gap regardless of thermal storage differences.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If two cities have identical sky view factors but different thermal mass or anthropogenic heat, and their nocturnal UHI differs significantly, geometry alone is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI is strongest in the early evening (within 2-3 hours of sunset), thermal storage release rather than steady-state radiative trapping is the dominant mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If high-altitude cities with deep canyons show smaller gaps due to low atmospheric back-radiation, the pure geometry model fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"After sunset, cooling is dominated by net longwave radiation loss. In rural areas with high sky view, radiation escapes freely to the cold sky. In urban street canyons, outgoing longwave radiation from the surface is intercepted by opposing walls and re-radiated back, drastically reducing net radiative cooling. The mechanism is purely geometric: the lower the sky view factor, the more longwave radiation is trapped. Cross-city variance is thus governed by building height and street canyon geometry, which determine the sky view factor and the radiative trapping efficiency.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
